title: "BiAnnual Gatherings"

Growing up, and until my youngest son left for his missionary service, there was one constant fixture on our calendar: a bi-annual gathering held on the first Saturday evening of April and October.

For nearly 80 years—from 1944 until 2021—these Saturday night Priesthood sessions were a highly anticipated events for male members of the Church. A time to gather as a family and a community, around the globe. An unique, on-line gathering, entirely voluntary.

With a focus on our responsibilities in the home, the Church, and the broader community.

Over the four decades, I experienced that tradition in every stage of life: first as a young missionary in Los Angeles, then as a new father learning the ropes, and eventually as a dad sitting alongside my teenage sons as they prepared for their own adult responsibilities.

One session in particular remains memorable.

My father, my three sons, and I made a trip into downtown Salt Lake City. We had dinner together at an American-Japanese restaurant before making our way toward Temple Square.

My dad was 86 at the time.

While he could still walk with a cane, he graciously allowed us to use a wheelchair so he could keep pace with our schedule.

That moment I learned a lesson about aging: flexibility and humility are part of growing old, but when accepted with gratitude, they allow the gathering with posterity and for the memory to last.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Aside from taking a few commemorative photos outside the Tabernacle and inside in front of the iconic organ pipes, I don't recall much of what was said from the pulpit that night.

Public records show that the First Presidency—Thomas S. Monson, Henry B. Eyring, and Dieter F. Uchtdorf—all spoke, and Elder Jeffrey R. Holland delivered a message on the responsibility of leaders to care personally for individuals and families.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

As a young man in South Korea, my father—originally a Northerner—had answered the call to serve as a soldier for a newly divided country.

He later built the financial foundation that enabled not only his own family to thrive, but his sibling's family as well.

Then, in his forties, he embraced both a new religion and a new country to further establish his family's future.

Throughout my formative, I don't remember my father sharing messages, instead I was able to witness someone who had lived through it and was still grateful.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

My father lived through a chaotic and tumultuous period in Korean history. Having survived those civil war years—at times through clear divine intervention—he emerged with less fear of the present or the future, and a deep, grounded dependence on deity. He had seen God rescue him from situations that were hopeless from a human perspective, and that built in him an enduring reservoir of faith.

I, on the other hand, grew up during a period of relative peace and rapid economic expansion, both in Korea and in the United States. Unlike my father, I never faced life-threatening crises to forge my faith. I do not carry that same trial-tested reservoir.

So what are my tools for the remainder of this journey? And what is my duty to impart to the next generation?

I have come to realize that faith is not only forged in crisis; it is also cultivated through quiet, unseen, steady fidelity—in regular personal and family devotion, and in the periodic gathering of men and women of faith. My responsibility is to pass down the principles that sustain a life of faith, home by home, day by day:

-   **Learn your duties as men.** Seek understanding and embrace accountability in every role you carry.

-   **Master yourself.** Bridle your passions and align your daily life with God’s commandments.

-   **Love your family unreservedly.** Love your wives and your children with the same selfless, enduring love that Jesus showed us.

-   **Answer the call to serve.** When opportunities arise to serve outside your own home—in the Church and in the community—step forward willingly.

-   **Endure to the end.** When your active days of service are complete, let your legacy be a blessing to your posterity—a living testament of someone who kept the faith.

I am deeply grateful for the opportunity to learn from the generation before me and leave meaningful lessons for the generation that follows. In a modern world that often feels disjointed and chaotic all over again, I am grateful to serve as a bridge.

Ultimately, legacy is more than just how we survived the trials of this world; it is about what we looked forward to, and prepared our family for, in the next phase of life.
